meta.status: DRAFT. Every entry is verified:false. Researched by web search; each motif entry names the page it rests on. The page reader used for research returned summaries, so quotes and details are unconfirmed until checked against the source. Entries starting 'DRAFT' rest on secondary sources (mostly Wikipedia) or on a wording the research could not confirm.
meta.coordsNote: All coordinates are approximate representative points for display only, not claimed origin points.
meta.dateRule: earliestRecordedDate is the earliest record we located, NOT the tale's origin. Most of these tales were oral long before they were written down; do not let the timeline imply otherwise.
meta.thompsonRule: Thompson ids were not checked against the Motif-Index itself. The ids shown were resolved against the trilogy dataset only. Confirm all ids in Thompson's index before use.
meta.pairTypeRule: connectionType is computed: same atuType family = cinderella-type parallel when the family is 510, otherwise thematic parallel. Where a story's atuType is marked 'verify', treat the pairing as unconfirmed.
meta.similarityRule: Shared motifs show similarity of story pattern. They are not evidence that one tale borrowed from or influenced another.

motifs.label: Mistreated by a cruel stepfamily or others
motifs.thompsonNote: S31 Cruel stepmother appears in the ATU 510A motif list (trilogy atu_seq); also used here for other cruelty, so the fit is loose
motifs.name: Unjust Treatment
motifs.description: A protagonist is wronged by family or others.
motifs.significance: Mistreatment sets up the conflict; the tales differ in who causes it and how it is answered.

motifs.label: Magical or supernatural helper
motifs.thompsonNote: B350 Grateful animals seen for tale type 480; other helper types (fairy, object, spirit): look up
motifs.name: Supernatural Assistance
motifs.description: Magical help arrives: a spirit, fairy or enchanted object.
motifs.significance: The helper differs widely between traditions; each story's entry says what it is.

motifs.label: Recognition through a lost or left-behind object
motifs.thompsonNote: H36.1 Slipper test seen in the ATU 510A list; ring/token recognition: look up in H0-H199 (identity tests: recognition)
motifs.name: Recognition Through a Lost Object
motifs.description: A lost object, like a shoe, identifies its owner.
motifs.significance: The object and what it proves differ: a shoe may lead to a bride, a ring may end a curse.

motifs.label: Impossible or dangerous tasks imposed
motifs.thompsonNote: H1010 Impossible tasks (Thompson H section); H935 Witch assigns tasks (type 480)
motifs.name: Impossible Tasks
motifs.description: The protagonist is set demanding or dangerous tasks.
motifs.significance: Tasks come from a stepfamily, a witch, a king or a god, and are met with help or cleverness.

motifs.label: Trickster or cunning hero
motifs.thompsonNote: look up (A500s culture hero, K deceptions)
motifs.name: Trickster
motifs.description: A cunning figure wins by trickery or disguise.
motifs.significance: Tricks are used to win something, escape danger or defeat a powerful rival.

motifs.label: Transformation or shapeshifting
motifs.name: Transformation
motifs.description: A person or object changes form.
motifs.significance: Shape-changes serve different ends in different tales: disguise, enchantment, punishment or revelation.

motifs.label: Death followed by rebirth or return
motifs.thompsonNote: look up in section E (The Dead)
motifs.name: Death & Rebirth
motifs.description: A character dies and returns, in the same or another form.
motifs.significance: In each tale the return from death works differently.

motifs.label: Miraculous or otherworldly birth or origin
motifs.name: Unusual Birth
motifs.description: A hero is born in an unusual way.
motifs.significance: How the character comes into the world is part of the story's wonder.

motifs.label: Lovers or kin separated, then reunited
motifs.thompsonNote: S451 Outcast wife at last united with husband and children seen for type 706; loose fit for several tales here
motifs.name: Separation & Reunion
motifs.description: Those who belong together part, then reunite.
motifs.significance: The cause and length of the separation, and whether the reunion is complete, differ in each story.

motifs.label: Lowly hero or heroine rises to high status
motifs.thompsonNote: L162 Lowly heroine marries prince seen in type listings; male counterpart: look up
motifs.name: Reversal of Fortune
motifs.description: A lowly or wronged character rises in status.
motifs.significance: The rise comes through marriage, reward or victory, depending on the tale.

motifs.label: Memory lost through a curse or enchantment
motifs.thompsonNote: look up (curses and forgetting, D/E sections)
motifs.name: Memory & Forgetting
motifs.significance: Only one tale in this atlas carries this motif, so it links to no others here.

stories.title: Cendrillon (Perrault, 1697)
stories.atuNote: The ATU index (via the trilogy dataset) lists Cendrillon among the names of type 510A 'Cinderella'; Wikipedia gives the type name as 'Persecuted Heroine'. Confirm in Uther.
stories.dateSource: Perrault, Histoires ou contes du temps passe (Paris, 1697), per the bibliographic note on the Pitt/Ashliman page of the translation
stories.dateCaveat: Earliest of THIS version. Basile's 'La gatta Cenerentola' (1634) is an earlier European literary Cinderella, and Strabo's Rhodopis is often cited as an earlier analogue (both per Wikipedia).
stories.summary: A girl mistreated by her stepmother and stepsisters is helped by her godmother, a fairy, who turns a pumpkin and animals into a coach and attendants and gives her glass slippers, warning her to leave before midnight. She loses a slipper, it fits only her, and she forgives her sisters.

motifEntries.howItAppears: Her stepmother and stepsisters make her do the household drudgery; she sleeps in a garret on a straw bed and sits in the chimney corner among the cinders after her work.

evidence.title: Perrault, Cinderella; or, The Little Glass Slipper (Pitt, Ashliman)

motifEntries.howItAppears: Her godmother, who is a fairy, magically provides a coach, attendants and glass slippers.

evidence.title: Perrault, Cinderella; or, The Little Glass Slipper (Pitt, Ashliman)

motifEntries.howItAppears: She loses a glass slipper as she leaves at midnight; when it is tried on her foot it fits her, and it fits no one else.

evidence.title: Perrault, Cinderella; or, The Little Glass Slipper (Pitt, Ashliman)

motifEntries.howItAppears: DRAFT, check what the mice and lizards become: a pumpkin becomes the coach and a rat becomes a coachman; the godmother also transforms mice and lizards into her retinue.

evidence.title: Perrault, Cinderella; or, The Little Glass Slipper (Pitt, Ashliman)

motifEntries.howItAppears: DRAFT, confirm the wording of the ending: from household drudge she marries the prince.

evidence.title: Perrault, Cinderella; or, The Little Glass Slipper (Pitt, Ashliman)

droppedMotifs.reason: Only weakly supported (she flees at midnight and is found through the slipper); not a separation in the sense of the motif.

stories.title: Kongjwi and Patjwi
stories.tradition: Korean folktale (oral; later printed as a novel)
stories.atuType: 510 (similar; Korean type KT 450 per Wikipedia; verify)
stories.atuNote: English Wikipedia says the tale resembles ATU 510 and merits its own Korean type, KT 450; it cites the National Folk Museum encyclopedia, which could not be opened.
stories.dateSource: No verified first record. The earliest print the research found is a 1919 movable-type edition (per Korean Wikipedia; a weak source).
stories.dateCaveat: Passed down orally for generations before it was written; the 1919 edition is not the origin. Versions differ widely.
stories.form: oral tale, later printed novel; many variants
stories.summary: Following English Wikipedia, cross-checked with Korean Wikipedia: Kongjwi is mistreated by her stepmother and stepsister Patjwi, is given hard chores, and is helped by animals and a celestial maiden. She loses a shoe, a magistrate finds her by it and marries her. In widely told versions the story continues: Patjwi drowns her and takes her place, and Kongjwi returns in another form to reveal the truth.

motifEntries.howItAppears: DRAFT (Korean Wikipedia): after her mother's death she is mistreated by her stepmother and stepsister Patjwi.
DRAFT (Wikipedia): helpers include a cow, a tortoise or toad, sparrows and, in the English account, a celestial maiden; the helpers differ between the two accounts.
DRAFT (English Wikipedia): she is told to plow a field with a wooden hoe, fill a pot that has a hole, and hull a large sack of rice.
DRAFT (Wikipedia): she loses a shoe on a bridge, and the magistrate's test with the shoe shows it fits only her.
DRAFT (English Wikipedia): in the continuation, a golden lotus is turned back into Kongjwi.
DRAFT (Wikipedia): Patjwi drowns her, and she returns as a spirit and in another form to reveal the truth; the endings differ between versions.
DRAFT (Wikipedia): she marries the magistrate.

droppedMotifs.reason: Not clearly stated in the sources read beyond the drowning and restoration.

stories.sensitivity: Korean tale with many oral variants; present which version is followed.
verifyBeforeUse: Every entry here rests on Wikipedia only. Open the National Folk Museum of Korea entry (folkency.nfm.go.kr/en/topic/detail/5996) and find a scholarly source
Confirm the earliest print edition (1919 per Korean Wikipedia) and the KT 450 claim
No source says the cow is black or names the draft's earlier 'Sinjeung Dongguk Yeoji Seungnam' woodblock editions; that earlier claim is unsupported
Choose which ending to present

stories.title: Ye Xian
stories.tradition: Tang-dynasty literary record of an oral tale, in Duan Chengshi's Youyang Zazu
stories.atuNote: An earlier project draft cited Ting's index via Wikipedia for 510A; this research pass opened no source that states an ATU number for Ye Xian. Confirm before treating the pairing with Cendrillon as established.
stories.dateSource: Youyang Zazu (Duan Chengshi, 803-863), continuation, juan 1; dates per medievalists.net and Wikipedia, which disagree (c. 850, 850-860, c. 860)
stories.dateCaveat: Earliest known written record, not the origin. The text credits an informant (Li Shiyuan, a former household servant of Duan's, per the text), so it circulated orally before.
stories.form: literary record of an oral tale
stories.summary: After her father, a cave chief, dies, Ye Xian is mistreated by her stepmother. She raises a fish that the stepmother kills; its bones grant wishes. At the cave festival she wears clothes and golden shoes provided through the bones and leaves one shoe behind. Cave people sell it to the kingdom of Tuohan, whose king obtains it. The stepmother and her daughter are later killed by flying stones.

motifEntries.howItAppears: After her father's death she is mistreated by her stepmother.
The bones of her dead fish grant whatever she asks of them.
For the festival, the bones provide fine blue-green clothing and golden shoes.
DRAFT, confirm in a translation that only her foot fits: she leaves one shoe behind at the festival; cave people sell it to the kingdom of Tuohan, and its king obtains it.
DRAFT, from a page summary only; confirm in the text: she is taken by the king as his chief wife.

droppedMotifs.reason: Not clearly stated.
Only Wikipedia's Cinderella article says the fish is the heroine's mother reincarnated; the Chinese text read does not confirm it.

verifyBeforeUse: Read Waley (Folklore 58, 1947) or Beauchamp's translation (Oral Tradition 25(2), 2010); neither could be opened
Confirm whether the text calls Tuohan an island and how the fish is described (red fins / golden eyes)
Do not call it 'the world's earliest Cinderella'; Rhodopis is usually cited earlier. Say 'among the earliest' or 'earliest surviving Asian version'
No ATU number was found in an opened source
stories.kind: Literary record of an oral tale

stories.title: Shakuntala (Kalidasa's play)
stories.tradition: Sanskrit court drama adapting an episode of the Mahabharata
stories.coordsNote: Placement unverified: the sources opened say only that Kanva's hermitage was on the Malini river in the Himalayan foothills. This is a display point.
stories.atuNote: Not a Cinderella-type tale. Display as a thematic parallel only.
stories.earliestRecordedDate: Kalidasa's play: c. 4th-5th century CE (uncertain; a minority view says 6th century)
stories.dateSource: Wikipedia: Kalidasa; Ryder's introduction to his translation (Gutenberg)
stories.dateCaveat: The Mahabharata episode is undated in the sources opened. The curse and the ring are not in the Mahabharata sections read (Adi Parva 70-74), so they appear to be Kalidasa's additions.
stories.summary: In Kalidasa's play, King Dushyanta marries Shakuntala, the foster daughter of the sage Kanva. After he leaves, the sage Durvasas's curse makes him forget her, to be lifted when he sees the token he gave her. The ring is lost while she worships at the Ganges, a fisherman finds it in a carp, the king's memory returns, and they are later reunited at the hermitage of Maricha.

motifEntries.howItAppears: In Kalidasa's play the curse is to be lifted when the king sees the token he gave her; the ring is lost while she worships at the Ganges, and a fisherman finds it in a carp.

evidence.title: Ryder, Kalidasa: Translations of Shakuntala and Other Works (Gutenberg), Acts IV and VI

motifEntries.howItAppears: In the play, Durvasas's curse makes the king forget her. In the Mahabharata, the king says he does not remember any union with her and no curse is mentioned.

evidence.title: Ryder translation (Gutenberg), Act IV; Mahabharata Adi Parva Section 74 (Wikisource)

motifEntries.howItAppears: DRAFT, reunion wording not confirmed: in Act VII the king travels to Gold Peak, the hermitage of Maricha, where the play ends.
In the Mahabharata she is the daughter of the apsara Menaka and the sage Viswamitra, left in the forest where birds protect her; Kanva adopts and names her.

droppedMotifs.reason: The draft's king torn between duty and love is not stated in the sections read; the only duty-related passage found is the marriage condition about their son's succession in the Mahabharata.

sources.title: Ryder, Kalidasa: Translations of Shakuntala and Other Works (Gutenberg #16659)

verifyBeforeUse: Check the Act VI wording about the ring and the place name, and the Act VII reunion, directly in the text
Kalidasa's date is genuinely uncertain; present it as a range
Where the hermitage was: only 'the Malini river, Himalayan foothills' is supported; Uttarakhand is not
Which details are Kalidasa's additions to the epic episode

stories.title: Vasilisa the Beautiful
stories.atuNote: English Wikipedia cites Haney for AT 480B* and Russian scholarship for SUS 480B* 'Stepmother and Stepdaughter'. Not a 510A tale. Second-hand; confirm in Haney (2014).
stories.earliestRecordedDate: 1855-1863 (Afanasyev's collection; the year of this tale is not verified)
stories.dateSource: A review of Afanasyev in the Journal of Folklore Research (IU); the English Wikipedia article on Afanasyev gives inconsistent dates (1855-1867, 1855-1863)
stories.dateCaveat: Collected from oral tradition and first printed by Afanasyev; some versions end differently.
stories.summary: After her mother's death, Vasilisa keeps a doll her mother gave her. Her stepmother's daughters send her to Baba Yaga for fire. With the doll's help she completes Baba Yaga's household tasks and is given a burning skull whose gaze destroys the stepfamily. She later spins and weaves very fine linen, and the Tsar, after receiving shirts made from it, marries her.

motifEntries.howItAppears: The stepmother's daughters put out the light and send Vasilisa to Baba Yaga to fetch fire.
The doll her mother gave her does the work for her, sifting the oats overnight and later producing the loom and the linen; Baba Yaga gives her the skull.

Baba Yaga sets her many household tasks, including cleaning the courtyard, cooking, sifting oats, sorting hay and making poppy-oil, which the doll helps her finish. 'Impossible' is the project's label for hard tasks.
She goes from persecuted orphan to wife of the Tsar, in the version read.

droppedMotifs.reason: No person or object changes form in the text read; the linen is very fine (it passes through a needle's eye) but not transformed.
Only her father's return is mentioned, and the reason for his absence was not read.

sources.title: Journal of Folklore Research review of Afanasyev

verifyBeforeUse: The Afanasyev number (No. 104) rests on Russian Wikipedia only
Confirm the exact tasks and the ending in the full Magnus text; the research read it through a summarizing page reader
The doll's mother's gift is a gift and a promise of safety in the text read; do not call it a 'blessing' unless the text does
ATU 480B* is second-hand

stories.title: How the Sky-god's Stories Came to Be Spider-stories (Anansi)
stories.tradition: Akan oral storytelling about Ananse, recorded by R. S. Rattray
stories.atuNote: No tale type found in an opened source.
stories.dateSource: Rattray, Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1930), tale 17, Akan text with English translation
stories.dateCaveat: The earliest record the research verified, not the earliest; a living oral tradition. Versions differ on which creatures are captured.
stories.form: oral tradition recorded by a colonial-era ethnographer
stories.summary: Ananse asks the Sky-god Nyankonpon for his stories and is told they can be had for nothing but the python, the leopard, the fairy and the hornets. On his wife Aso's advice, Ananse traps each by trickery and delivers them. The Sky-god accepts, and the tales come to be called Spider-stories.

motifEntries.howItAppears: Ananse traps the python by tying it to a palm branch, the hornets by coaxing them into a water gourd, the leopard with a pit, and the fairy with a sticky doll holding mashed yam.

evidence.title: Rattray, Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales (1930), tale 17 (Internet Archive full text)

motifEntries.howItAppears: The Sky-god says the stories cannot be bought for anything except the python, the leopard, the fairy and the hornets. 'Impossible' is the project's label for hard demands.

evidence.title: Rattray, Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales (1930), tale 17 (Internet Archive full text)

droppedMotifs.reason: Ananse is not shown low before; he gains the stories.
His wife Aso's advice is human, not supernatural; no 'golden chest' or silk ladder appears in Rattray's tale.

sources.title: Rattray, Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales (1930) (Internet Archive full text)

stories.sensitivity: A living Akan tradition, not a myth of the past. Rattray was a colonial-era British ethnographer; credit the Akan tradition and seek Ghanaian-authored tellings.
verifyBeforeUse: Confirm the tale number and exact details in the archive.org scan
Say which version is followed; others differ on the creatures and on who owns the stories
Add a Ghanaian-authored source
stories.originalTitle: Anansesem (Ananse stories), recorded by Rattray as tale 17

stories.title: Momotaro (Peach Boy)
stories.tradition: Japanese folktale (mukashibanashi), printed in Edo-period children's books and standardized in the Meiji era
stories.coordsNote: Okayama is traditionally associated with the tale, which the research did not verify. This is a display point.
stories.atuNote: No tale type found in an opened source.
stories.earliestRecordedDate: 1723 (oldest surviving printed text, a miniature akahon)
stories.dateSource: Wikipedia: Momotaro; National Diet Library JapanSearch page
stories.dateCaveat: Earlier Edo works (Genroku era, 1688-1704, or earlier) are lost per Wikipedia. An oral version may date to the Muromachi period (1392-1573). The version most people know was standardized in the Meiji era.
stories.form: oral tale, printed in Edo-period children's books
stories.summary: An old woman finds a large peach in the river, and when it is cut open a boy comes out. The couple raise him. When grown he sets off for the island of the devils with millet dumplings from his parents, which he gives to a dog, a monkey and a pheasant who join him. They defeat the devils' chief and return with the treasure.

motifEntries.howItAppears: He is born from a large peach that floats down the river and is cut open by the old woman.
A dog, a monkey and a pheasant join him after each is given a millet dumpling, and they help him defeat the devils.

droppedMotifs.reason: He becomes wealthy but there is no prior misfortune.
Only weakly supported: he leaves his parents and returns.
No source opened says filial duty is a theme.

stories.sensitivity: Wikipedia documents that Momotaro was used as a soldier figure in wartime propaganda from the 1890s through the Second World War, with the devils portrayed as enemies, and that the 1894 Meiji version, edited by Iwaya Sazanami, is the standardized form. Mention this when presenting the tale.
verifyBeforeUse: The text followed is an early-20th-century English translation of the Meiji form, not an Edo text; its translator is unnamed
Check the wartime-use claims in the primary scholarship (Dower, others); they come from Wikipedia here
Check the Edo texts for what the helpers are given (oldest texts differ on the dumplings)

stories.title: The Golden Crab
stories.tradition: Greek wonder tale published in German by Bernhard Schmidt (1877) and in English by Andrew Lang (1894)
stories.coordsNote: Place of collection not verified (a search summary suggested Zakynthos; that page was not opened). This is a representative Greek point.
stories.atuNote: English Wikipedia gives ATU 425D 'Vanished Husband learned of by keeping inn' and says Greek versions often combine it with 425E. In Lang's text the princess does not keep an inn.
stories.dateSource: Schmidt, Griechische Maerchen, Sagen und Volkslieder (Leipzig, 1877), per the footnote in Lang's Yellow Fairy Book and Wikipedia
stories.dateCaveat: Earliest record of this specific tale that the research verified, not its origin. Lang's English version is 1894.
stories.form: oral tale published by a collector
stories.summary: Following Lang's English text: a fisherman catches a talking golden crab, which has the fisherman's wife ask the king for his younger daughter and meets the king's demands with a golden rod. On the wedding night the crab says he is an enchanted prince, a crab by day and a man at night. When the princess's mother burns his crab-shell, he vanishes. Guided by an old man, the princess finds her husband among twelve enchanted eagles in an underground palace and they are reunited.

motifEntries.howItAppears: The crab's golden rod produces the flower-covered wall and the garden with fountains overnight, and a servant who comes out of a mountain or the garden gate supplies the golden garments and armour.

evidence.title: Lang, The Yellow Fairy Book, 'The Golden Crab' (Gutenberg #640)

motifEntries.howItAppears: The prince is enchanted to be a crab by day and a man at night, and he can turn into an eagle; twelve eagles become youths at a fountain.

evidence.title: Lang, The Yellow Fairy Book, 'The Golden Crab' (Gutenberg #640)

motifEntries.howItAppears: The king demands, each by the next morning, a wall higher than his tower covered in all the flowers of the world and then a garden with fountains of gold and jewels; the crab fulfils both with the golden rod.

evidence.title: Lang, The Yellow Fairy Book, 'The Golden Crab' (Gutenberg #640)

motifEntries.howItAppears: After the mother burns the shell her husband does not come back; the princess later finds him in an underground palace, recognizes him among the twelve, and embraces him.

evidence.title: Lang, The Yellow Fairy Book, 'The Golden Crab' (Gutenberg #640)

droppedMotifs.reason: She recognizes him by sight, not by an object.
Her loyalty is shown but no conflict with duty is stated.
Only weakly supported (the fisherman's household becomes rich).

sources.title: CU Boulder Fairy Tales project: The Golden Crab (summary)

stories.sensitivity: Lang's text uses dated language for a servant character; avoid repeating it uncritically.
verifyBeforeUse: Open Schmidt's 1877 book to confirm the tale number, narrator and place of collection
ATU 425D is Wikipedia-only
No golden hen, spindle or cross-continental journey appears in this tale; earlier draft claims about them are unsupported

stories.title: Urashima Taro
stories.tradition: Japanese legend first recorded in 8th-century chronicles and poetry and reshaped in the Muromachi-era Otogizoshi
stories.atuNote: English Wikipedia gives ATU 681 'The Relativity of Time' and Ikeda's Japanese index type 470*; Wikipedia only.
stories.earliestRecordedDate: early 8th century CE (Tango Fudoki, c. 713, extant only in fragment; Man'yoshu 9.1740; Nihon Shoki entry)
stories.dateSource: Wikipedia: Urashima Taro; Univie Kamigraphie on the Man'yoshu poem; Hearn and Chamberlain's retellings (Gutenberg)
stories.dateCaveat: These are the earliest surviving records, not the origin. The Nihon Shoki entry is conventionally dated to the reign of Yuryaku (478); the Fudoki is preserved only as a quoted fragment. Versions differ on whether the hero rescues or catches the turtle and on how many years pass.
stories.form: legend recorded in chronicles and poetry, reshaped in later tellings
stories.summary: In the earliest versions a fisherman called Urashima meets a woman from the immortal land of Tokoyo; in the Tango Fudoki she is a turtle he caught. He lives there about three years, returns to find his home and village gone, and opening the box she gave him ends in her loss or his own aging. Later tellings add a rescued turtle and a Dragon Palace.

motifEntries.howItAppears: DRAFT (Wikipedia and Univie): in the Fudoki a turtle he caught becomes a woman who takes him to the realm of the immortals; in the Man'yoshu the sea god's daughter takes him to the Land Everlasting.
DRAFT (Wikipedia and Chamberlain): in the earliest accounts a caught turtle becomes a woman; in later versions the hero ages when the box is opened.

droppedMotifs.reason: The sources describe a time gap, not memory loss.
In the early versions the woman is carried away; no reunion except a later shared revering as deities in the Otogizoshi per Wikipedia.

sources.title: Univie Kamigraphie: Urashima Taro in the Man'yoshu

verifyBeforeUse: The Nihon Shoki and Fudoki details come from Wikipedia only; open a scholarly edition
Years passed differ by source (about 300 in the Fudoki, 700 in the Otogizoshi, 400 in Chamberlain); say which version is followed
The tamatebako box appears only in a poem inserted into the Otogizoshi texts; early sources have a comb-box
ATU 681 and Ikeda 470* are Wikipedia-only

stories.title: Sedna (Nuliajuk, Takannaaluk)
stories.region: Inuit Nunangat and Greenland (Boas recorded it on Baffin Island)
stories.dateSource: Franz Boas, The Central Eskimo (Sixth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, 1884-1885, published 1888), text pp. 583-587
stories.dateCaveat: Earliest full text the research verified, recorded by an outside ethnographer; the story is oral and far older. Versions differ greatly by region (Cumberland Sound, Igloolik, Netsilik, Greenland).
stories.form: oral tradition recorded by an ethnologist
stories.summary: Following Boas's 'Sedna and the Fulmar' (Baffin Island): Sedna, who has refused every suitor, is lured away by a fulmar who promises a rich home but delivers a miserable tent. Her father kills the fulmar and takes her away by boat; the other fulmars raise a storm and the father throws her overboard and cuts off her clinging fingers. The finger joints become whales and seals. Other Inuit tellings differ in key ways.

motifEntries.howItAppears: In Boas's version the fulmar deceives her, and her father throws her overboard and cuts off her fingers to save himself.

evidence.title: Boas, The Central Eskimo (Gutenberg #42084), 'Sedna and the Fulmar'

motifEntries.howItAppears: In Boas's version the cut-off finger joints fall into the sea and become whales and seals, and the stumps become bearded seals.

droppedMotifs.reason: Nothing helps Sedna in Boas's version.
She is separated from her father, but the reunion in the text is violent and the motif's meaning does not fit.

stories.sensitivity: A living Inuit belief and story. Prefer Inuit-authored tellings (for example Inhabit Media's books) over Boas's 1880s ethnography, use 'Inuit' (not 'Eskimo'), and take care with her names, many of which are avoidance names. Do not merge variants.
verifyBeforeUse: Walrus origin and hair-combing are not in Boas's Sedna text; they come from other and secondary tellings (for example Igloolik). Add them only from a sourced Inuit telling
Check the Canadian Museum of History, Inuit Cultural Online Resource and Rasmussen, which could not be opened
Name the nation or region for the version used

stories.title: Rhodopis and the eagle-stolen sandal
stories.tradition: Greek-language ancient literary tradition about a Greek woman in Egypt
stories.atuNote: Often called an early analogue of Cinderella (Wikipedia: 'sometimes considered the earliest known version'); no ATU number from an opened source, so it is not paired as a Cinderella-type tale.
stories.earliestRecordedDate: late 1st century BCE to early 1st century CE (Strabo, Geographica 17.1.33)
stories.dateSource: Strabo; the date of his Geographica is disputed (a first edition around 7 BCE and a final edition no later than 23 CE, per Wikipedia)
stories.dateCaveat: Earliest surviving written record of the sandal story, not its origin. Herodotus (5th century BCE) records Rhodopis herself but no sandal story.
stories.summary: Following Strabo: while the courtesan Rhodopis (called Doricha by Sappho) was bathing, an eagle took one of her sandals and carried it to Memphis, dropping it in the lap of the king as he gave judgment outdoors. The king, struck by the sandal, sent men everywhere to find its owner. They found her at Naucratis, and he made her his wife. Strabo does not name the king.

motifEntries.howItAppears: In Strabo the king sends men out to find the owner of the sandal the eagle dropped, and she is found at Naucratis. Strabo does not say the sandal was fitted to her foot.
In Strabo a courtesan becomes the king's wife; in Herodotus she is a Thracian slave ransomed by Charaxus who grows rich in Egypt.

droppedMotifs.reason: Only weak: an eagle carries the sandal. Strabo does not call it divine, and no source opened links it to Horus.
Strabo shows no mistreatment; Herodotus has her as a slave who works as a courtesan but frames no injustice.

verifyBeforeUse: Read Strabo 17.1.33 directly (the research saw a summary); check whether he calls her queen of Egypt
Aelian (Varia Historia 13.33) names the king Psammetichus; not opened. Herodotus places her under Amasis. Strabo names no king and does not say Pharaoh
Do not call her an 'enslaved laundress' or the sandal 'gilded' or 'rose-red'; none of that is in Strabo
Say 'sometimes considered the earliest known Cinderella-type story', not 'the oldest precursor'

stories.title: Blessing or Property (a Swahili one-handed-girl tale)
stories.tradition: Swahili tale recorded by Edward Steere in Swahili Tales as Told by Natives of Zanzibar (1870)
stories.atuNote: Wikipedia gives ATU 706 'The Maiden Without Hands'. Steere does not classify it. This is not a Cinderella-type (510) tale.
stories.dateSource: Steere, Swahili Tales as Told by Natives of Zanzibar (London: Bell and Daldy, 1870), per the Wikisource title page
stories.dateCaveat: The earliest record the research verified, not the origin. The wider tale type is much older and widely known in Europe. Steere says the sources of his tales are uncertain.
stories.form: oral tale recorded by a missionary-scholar
stories.summary: Following Steere's 'Blessing or Property': a dying father asks his two children whether they want blessing or property. The brother takes the property and the sister the blessing, and she is left a pot and a mortar. When she refuses to sell him pumpkins, the brother cuts off her hand and drives her out. A snake she helped restores her hand and gives her a ring that provides food and a house. A king's son marries her, the brother has her cast out as a witch, and she is reunited with her husband after telling her story.

motifEntries.howItAppears: The brother takes the property, cuts off her right hand and drives her from the house; later he denounces her to the king as a witch and she is cast out.

evidence.title: Steere, Swahili Tales: Blessing or Property (Wikisource)

motifEntries.howItAppears: A snake she sheltered leads her to its home, where her hand is restored; its father's ring can produce food, clothing or a house, and she uses it to build a home.

evidence.title: Steere, Swahili Tales: Blessing or Property (Wikisource)

motifEntries.howItAppears: From destitute and maimed she becomes a prince's wife with a house built by the ring; at the end her brother is banished.

evidence.title: Steere, Swahili Tales: Blessing or Property (Wikisource)

motifEntries.howItAppears: The king's family expels her and her son while the prince is away; he returns to find graves prepared for them, and at the end she tells her story and he embraces her.

evidence.title: Steere, Swahili Tales: Blessing or Property (Wikisource)

droppedMotifs.reason: No object identifies her; recognition comes from her telling her story.

stories.title: The Story of Tam and Cam
stories.tradition: Vietnamese folktale; related variants among other peoples in Vietnam are noted by Wikipedia
stories.coordsNote: No opened source locates the tale's origin; it is told across Vietnam. This is an approximate national display point (Landes's informants were from Nghe An province).
stories.atuNote: No opened source states an ATU number. Wikipedia places it only in the 'ATU 500-559' range; a search-result snippet attributed 510A to SurLaLune, but that page could not be opened. Treat the Cinderella-type pairing as unconfirmed.
stories.dateSource: A. Landes, 'Histoire de con Tam et de con Cam', in Contes et legendes annamites (Saigon: Imprimerie coloniale, 1886), ch. XXII, pp. 52-57; EBSCO Research Starters calls it 'the earliest European transcription'; the Internet Archive record confirms the book
stories.dateCaveat: The earliest record the research verified, not the origin. 'Earliest European transcription' leaves open earlier non-European versions; whether the tale appeared in the journal Excursions et Reconnaissances (1884-1887) before the book is unverified. Landes recorded his tales through intermediaries, shortened them, and swapped the sisters' names relative to the standard version.
stories.form: oral tale first transcribed by a European colonial administrator; many variants
stories.summary: Following the standard version as summarised by Wikipedia and EBSCO: Tam, mistreated by her stepmother, is cheated of her catch by her half-sister Cam. A spirit-helper tells her to bury the bones of her fish in four jars, which later provide clothes and a horse for the king's festival. She loses a slipper on a bridge, it fits only her, and she marries the king. She is then killed and reborn several times, as a bird, trees and a golden fruit, until the king recognizes her work and she returns.

motifEntries.howItAppears: DRAFT (Wikipedia): the heroine is overworked by her stepmother while her half-sister does no chores, and the half-sister secretly steals her fishing catch.

motifEntries.howItAppears: DRAFT (Wikipedia): a spirit-helper advises her about the fish and its bones, and the buried bones produce clothes, a horse and a saddle.

motifEntries.howItAppears: DRAFT (Wikipedia): a slipper lost on a stone bridge fits only the heroine, so the king identifies and marries her; later the king recognizes her by the betel quids she prepared.

motifEntries.howItAppears: DRAFT (Wikipedia): she is killed by a fall from an areca tree and is reborn through bird, tree and fruit forms until she regains human shape.

stories.sensitivity: A living tradition that is part of Vietnam's cultural heritage. The original ending is violent (the stepmother unknowingly eats her daughter's flesh); EBSCO says Vietnam's 2011 school textbook removed that scene, so a children-facing summary should say Cam is punished. Landes's 1886 text was recorded through intermediaries under colonial administration and swaps the sisters' names; Judy Sierra's 1992 English translation repeated the swap. Do not call it purely Vietnamese in origin without a source; EBSCO links the slipper motif to Rhodopis and a route through the Middle East, India and China, but that is only EBSCO's claim.

stories.title: Hunahpu and Xbalanque, the Hero Twins (Popol Vuh)
stories.earliestRecordedDate: 1554-1558 (K'iche' text in Latin script; the original is lost)
stories.dateSource: Christenson's introduction to his translation of the Popol Vuh (Mesoweb edition)
stories.dateCaveat: The oldest surviving copy is Francisco Ximenez's, made in 1701-1704, with a parallel Spanish translation. The text records older oral tradition; the tale is older than any written record.
stories.summary: Following Christenson's translation: the twins' father and uncle were killed by the lords of Xibalba. Hunahpu and Xbalanque, conceived when their father's skull spat in their mother's hand, go down to Xibalba and survive a ball game and trials in the Houses of Blade, Cold, Jaguars, Fire and Bats. They allow their own deaths, are ground up in a river and return, first as fish-like people and then as poor orphan dancers, trick the lords into asking to be sacrificed, and defeat Xibalba. Afterward one rises as the sun and the other as the moon.

motifEntries.howItAppears: Their half-brothers abuse them out of envy, and the lords of Xibalba killed their father and uncle; the twins call themselves the avengers of their fathers.

Ants steal flowers from the lords' garden, and an insect (really a hair plucked from Hunahpu's knee) learns the lords' names on the road to Xibalba; Xbalanque calls animals to help when Hunahpu is beheaded.
After their deaths they appear first as fish-like people and then as ragged orphan dancers; their half-brothers become spider monkeys; at the end they rise as the sun and the moon.
The lords of Xibalba, who killed the twins' father and thought the twins defeated, are themselves sacrificed and told they will never again be great.
The lords set deadly trials: nights in the Houses of Blade, Cold, Jaguars, Fire and Bats, and a ball game. 'Impossible' is the project's label for lethal trials.
Disguised as orphan dancers, the twins feign sacrifice and revival and persuade the lords to ask to be sacrificed, and the lords are killed and not revived.
The twins jump into a pit oven, their bones are ground and strewn in the river, and on the fifth day they appear again as fish-like people.
Their mother is made pregnant when the skull of One Hunahpu spits into her hand and tells her his son is like his spittle.

droppedMotifs.reason: Only weak support (honoring their father's skull).
Only weak support (the lords' names are learned and their father's name is not to be forgotten).
Filial duty appears in the twins' speeches, but the motif's duty-versus-love sense is not shown.

sources.title: Christenson, Popol Vuh (Mesoweb electronic edition of the 2003 University of Oklahoma Press translation)

stories.sensitivity: A K'iche' Maya sacred text that remains meaningful to living K'iche' people. Christenson is an outside scholar who worked with K'iche' collaborators. Do not call the lords of Xibalba 'demons'; use 'K'iche'' and 'Maya' spellings and prefer K'iche' sources.

The sun and moon ending is in Christenson; check Tedlock, and any Venus identification, which was not found
Ximenez's copy is dated 1701-1704 (Christenson) or c. 1701 (Wikipedia); pick one

stories.title: The Fisherman and the Jinni
stories.tradition: Arabian Nights (Thousand and One Nights) frame-tale cycle, Syrian recension
stories.coordsNote: The text names no real home for the fisherman, only a seashore, a mountain tarn and an unnamed city. This is a display point for the Nights tradition (Baghdad), not the tale's setting or origin.
stories.atuType: 331 (per Wikipedia citing the Arabian Nights Encyclopedia; verify)
stories.atuNote: English Wikipedia gives ATU 331 'The Spirit in the Bottle'; the primary reference was not opened.
stories.earliestRecordedDate: by the 14th-15th century CE (Galland manuscript, BnF arabe 3609-3611)
stories.dateSource: The tale is in the contents of the Galland (Syrian) manuscript, per a list of its contents and Wikipedia; dating is disputed: Zotenberg and Mahdi say 14th century, Grotzfeld argues it was not copied before about 1450
stories.dateCaveat: The earliest surviving manuscript record of the tale, not its origin. The oldest Nights witness overall is a 9th-century fragment, which is not this tale.
stories.summary: Following Burton's translation: a poor old fisherman hauls up a copper jar sealed with Solomon's seal. A jinni who has sworn to kill whoever frees him comes out, and the fisherman tricks him back into the jar by doubting that he could fit. The jinni swears a covenant and leads him to a tarn with four coloured fish, which earn the fisherman 400 dinars from the sultan and begin the story of an enchanted prince.

motifEntries.howItAppears: After being freed, the jinni leads the fisherman to a tarn where he catches four coloured fish that earn him payment.

evidence.title: Burton, The Fisherman and the Jinni (sacred-texts mirror)

motifEntries.howItAppears: The fisherman asks how the jinni could fit in so small a vessel, and when the jinni goes back into the jar he seals it again.

evidence.title: Burton, The Fisherman and the Jinni (sacred-texts mirror)

motifEntries.howItAppears: The jinni turns to vapor to enter the jar, and the enchanted prince is found half man and half stone.
